findings.guidance:
The json type has no equality operator, so existing queries that use
SELECT DISTINCT, GROUP BY, or comparisons on the column start failing. jsonb
is also faster to process and indexable.

  ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN settings jsonb;
findings.statement:
CREATE TABLE users (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  email varchar(255) NOT NULL,
  name text,
  settings json
)

findings.guidance:
Running application code (and ORM/sqlc-generated code with cached column lists)
still references the column and fails once it is gone.

Safe sequence:
  1. Remove every read and write of the column from the application and deploy.
  2. Then, in a later migration, drop the column:

     ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;

If the column is already unused, add "-- safe_sql:disable ban-drop-column"
above the statement to acknowledge this.
findings.statement: ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name

findings.message: adding column users.token with volatile default gen_random_uuid()
findings.statement: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN token uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()

findings.message: creating index users_token_idx on users without CONCURRENTLY
findings.guidance:
CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock on the table, blocking writes until the index
is built. Build it concurrently instead:

  CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email ON users (email);

CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction, so the migration file must opt
out of the tool's transaction wrapper (see concurrent-index-in-transaction).
Note that a concurrent build that fails leaves an INVALID index behind that
must be dropped before retrying.

findings.message: SET NOT NULL on users.email without a validated CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) constraint
findings.statement: ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL

findings.message: UPDATE on users in a migration that also changes schema
findings.guidance:
An UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE that touches many rows in the same migration (and
transaction) as schema changes keeps the DDL locks held until the data change
finishes, and a single large statement can take a long time on its own.

Backfill in a separate step, outside the schema migration, in batches:

  UPDATE users SET status = 'active' WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2;  -- loop over ranges

If the table is small or the migration is a one-row seed, add
"-- safe_sql:disable ban-dml-in-migration" above the statement.
findings.statement: UPDATE users SET token = gen_random_uuid() WHERE token IS NULL
